50.title: Eight handfuls of grass
50.hook: a grass-cutter gives him grass; he makes a seat beneath the tree, facing east
50.howItsDone: Pilgrims visit the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya, in India, to sit and meditate beneath it, and some Buddhists keep a dedicated seat or cushion at home for daily practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neranjara: the golden bowl floating upstream, against the current. Now a new week begins: the night under the tree.

A chair at the kitchen table where the bills get paid. The edge of a bed where the hard phone calls get made. A back step for thinking. Homes collect places like these without anyone deciding on them. Where a person sits can tell the body what's about to happen. It's late afternoon on the day of Sujata's milk-rice. The wanderer is walking toward a great fig tree near the river. On the way, a man comes along the path carrying freshly cut grass. His name, the telling says, is Sotthiya.
screen: `THE PLACE YOU SIT WHEN IT MATTERS.` → `WALKING TOWARD A GREAT FIG TREE.` → `A MAN CARRYING GRASS.`

segments.voice: Sotthiya the grass-cutter sees the wanderer and, without being asked, offers him eight handfuls of grass. A small gift, the kind you'd give without thinking. The wanderer accepts it and carries it to the tree. It's a fig, the kind called assattha, or pipal, with broad, heart-shaped leaves that tremble in the slightest breeze. Soon it will have a new name: the Bodhi tree, the tree of awakening. Tradition holds that a descendant of it grows at that spot today, in Bodh Gaya, in India, where pilgrims come to sit beneath it. The telling says he walks around the tree, looking for the right place. On the south side, the ground seems to tilt. He tries the west, then the north. Then he stands on the east side, and the earth feels steady. There. He spreads the grass on the ground and sits on it, cross-legged, his back to the trunk, facing east, toward where the sun will rise. That's all that happens today. A man takes a gift of grass and makes a seat. But Buddhists keep telling this small moment because of what a seat means. You can think about doing something forever. The moment you sit down to do it, you've decided. And the telling gives this seat a name of its own: the unconquered seat.

segments.voice: Make a seat right where you are, a cushion, a folded blanket, a chair, the edge of the bed, arranged on purpose the way the wanderer spread his grass, facing east or toward the light if you can. Sit down slowly, knowing you're sitting, and feel the seat take your weight: the backs of the legs, the sit bones, the feet on the floor, the spine rising easy and upright. Then just sit.
Assattha. The pipal fig tree where the wanderer spread a grass-cutter's gift of grass as his seat, facing east.
Your line: a seat is a decision. Yours can be any chair at all. Fifty days now.

51.title: "I will not rise"
51.hook: he resolves not to move until he awakens
51.howItsDone: Some Buddhist meditators begin a sit or a retreat by making a quiet resolve (adhitthana) to stay for a set time, and resolve is counted among the perfections in Theravada teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday, assattha, the fig tree: a grass-cutter's gift spread as a seat facing east. A seat is a decision.

A workout you'll quit if it gets too hard. A writing session with the phone face-up beside you. Ten minutes of meditation, and at minute four a voice says, you know, that's probably enough. An exit built into everything can feel safe. It also means never finding out what's on the other side of staying. The wanderer is sitting on his seat of grass under the great fig tree, facing east. The sun is going down. And before the night begins, he makes a vow.
screen: `AN EXIT BUILT INTO EVERYTHING.` → `AT MINUTE FOUR...` → `A VOW AT SUNSET.`

segments.voice: The later telling gives the vow in dramatic words. Let my skin and sinews and bones dry up. Let the flesh and blood in my body wither. But I will not rise from this seat until I have found complete awakening. It sounds like the old austerities, but it isn't. He's not starving now; he's eaten. He's not forcing his breath. He's just decided not to leave. That difference, forcing or staying, is the whole lesson of the last two weeks. The Pali canon has a similar resolve in the Buddha's own words: let only skin and sinews and bones remain, but my effort will not slacken until I reach what can be reached. And what he's staying for has a name: bodhi. It means awakening, from a root, budh, that means to wake up, to become aware, to understand. The same root is in the word Buddha, which comes soon. In Buddhist teaching, bodhi is not a trance, or a vision, or a feeling of bliss. It's pictured as waking up, the way you wake from a dream and see the room as it actually is. That's why the tree became the Bodhi tree, and the place Bodh Gaya. Staying put, in Buddhist practice, doesn't mean gritting your teeth through pain. It means not running. When restlessness says get up, you notice it, and stay. When boredom says check your phone, you notice it, and stay. The noticing is the practice.

segments.voice: Make a small vow, the size of today: for these two minutes, I'll stay, not perfectly still, not perfectly calm, just here. When the mind says that's enough, notice it and stay; when an itch comes, see if it passes; when a thought pulls you away, come back to the breath. You're not fighting anything, just not leaving.
Bodhi. Awakening, from the root budh, to wake up. What the wanderer vowed not to rise without, and the name of the tree he sat beneath.
Your line: stay put. The night under the tree is just beginning. See you there tomorrow.

52.title: Mara's army
52.hook: Mara comes with storms and armies, then his daughters; the arrows fall as flowers
52.howItsDone: Buddhist temple murals show Mara's army and the weapons turning to flowers, and some meditation teachers speak of noticing 'Mara' in the mind's own distractions, naming them without obeying them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bodhi: awakening, and the vow, I will not rise from this seat. Stay put.

You sit down to be quiet for two minutes, and the attack begins. Not from outside. From inside. The email you forgot to send. The thing someone said last week. Your knee. A sudden craving for something sweet. A voice that says this is pointless, who do you think you are. The moment you decide to stay, everything that wants you to leave can seem to show up at once. Under the tree, the wanderer has made his vow. And the old tellings say that the moment he did, someone noticed. Someone who had been waiting since the palace gate.
screen: `THE ATTACK BEGINS FROM INSIDE.` → `EVERYTHING THAT WANTS YOU TO LEAVE.` → `SOMEONE NOTICED.`

segments.voice: Mara. The name comes from the same root as marana, death. Mara is the one who kills, or the one who keeps you in the cycle of death and rebirth. Buddhists speak of him as a god-like tempter, and also as a picture of everything in the mind that resists waking up. The later telling makes the attack enormous. Mara rides out on a giant elephant with an army stretching to the horizon, every soldier armed. He sends storms: wind, then rain, rocks, weapons, burning coals, hot ash, sand, mud, and darkness. And everything he throws turns into flowers and perfume, drifting down around the seated man like offerings. In some tellings, Mara's three daughters come too, beautiful, to tempt him. In a sutta, they arrive after the awakening instead, and fail just the same. But in a poem in the Sutta Nipata, in the Pali canon, the Buddha names Mara's army himself, and its soldiers live closer to home. Your first army, he tells Mara, is sensual desire. The second, discontent. The third, hunger and thirst. The fourth, craving. The fifth, sloth and drowsiness. The sixth, fear. The seventh, doubt. The eighth, hypocrisy and stubbornness. The ninth, gain and fame and honor wrongly won. The tenth, praising yourself and looking down on others. Not demons on elephants. Discontent, fear, doubt, the need to be seen. In the poem, he doesn't run; he says he will break this army with wisdom, the way a stone breaks an unbaked clay pot. In the later telling, he doesn't even move. He stays on the seat, and everything thrown at him falls like petals.

segments.voice: As you sit, watch for Mara's army, and when something arrives to pull you off the seat, name it softly: wanting, doubt, boredom, fear, drowsiness. Don't fight it and don't obey it; picture it landing near you like a petal, let it lie there, and come back to the breath. The next one will come; name it too.
Mara. The tempter, whose name comes from death, who attacked the wanderer with storms and armies that fell as flowers.
Your line: the arrows become flowers. The night isn't over yet. Day fifty-two is yours.

53.title: Touching the earth
53.hook: Mara asks who witnesses his right to that seat; he touches the ground, and the earth answers
53.howItsDone: The earth-touching gesture (bhumisparsha mudra) is one of the most common poses in Buddhist statues, and in Southeast Asia many temples honor the earth goddess who wrings the waters of merit from her hair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mara: the tempter whose storms and weapons fell as flowers. The arrows become flowers.

Have you ever been asked, out loud, what gives you the right? What makes you think you can do this job, hold this opinion, take up this space? It's one of the oldest weapons there is. It doesn't hurt the body. It goes straight for whether you belong. Mara's army has failed; the rocks and arrows have fallen as flowers. So Mara stops attacking and starts arguing. This seat, he says, belongs to me. Who are you to sit there? His whole army roars behind him: we are his witnesses! Now, who is yours?
screen: `WHAT GIVES YOU THE RIGHT?` → `THIS SEAT BELONGS TO ME.` → `WHO IS YOUR WITNESS?`

segments.voice: It's a lonely question. Mara has a whole army to speak for him. The wanderer is alone under a tree at night. In the telling, he answers that no living being is present to be his witness. But across countless lives, he says, he has given and given, practicing generosity and patience again and again. Then he moves his right hand. He draws it out from his lap, lets it rest over his right knee, and touches the ground with his fingertips. The earth itself will speak for him. And the earth answers, the telling says, with a roar like thunder: I am his witness. Mara's elephant kneels. The army scatters. Southeast Asia adds a beloved scene: the earth appears as a goddess, wrings out her long hair, and from it pours all the water of his past good deeds, a flood that sweeps Mara's army away. You'll see her in temples in Thailand, Cambodia, Laos and Myanmar. And the gesture is everywhere. Check the right hand on almost any seated Buddha statue. If it's reaching down to touch the ground, that's this moment: the earth-touching gesture, maybe the most common pose in all of Buddhist art. When someone asks what gives you the right, you don't have to shout louder. You can put your hand on the ground. The earth under you, and the good you've actually done, is witness enough.
screen: `NO ONE HERE TO SPEAK FOR HIM.` · `HIS HAND REACHES TO THE GROUND.` · `THE EARTH ROARS: I AM HIS WITNESS.` · `THE MOST COMMON POSE IN ART.` · then, large: `THE EARTH IS YOUR WITNESS.`

segments.voice: Reach down and touch the ground with your right hand: the floor, the grass, the carpet, or, if you can't reach, press your feet firmly into the floor. Feel it, solid, holding you up, asking nothing, and bring to mind one good thing you have actually done; small is fine, a kindness, an honest word, a promise kept. Let the ground and that memory be your witnesses; right now, you don't need anyone else to vouch for you.
Bhūmisparśa. The earth-touching gesture: the wanderer's right hand reaching down to call the earth as his witness, now carved on countless Buddha statues.
Your line: the earth is your witness. The hand on the ground says it without a word. That's day fifty-three.

54.title: The three watches
54.hook: first watch, his past lives; second, beings passing by their deeds; third, the ending of the taints (MN 36)
54.howItsDone: Buddhists teach the three knowledges of the awakening night (past lives, the passing of beings according to kamma, and the ending of the taints), and some communities keep all-night vigils of meditation on the anniversary of the awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhūmisparśa: the hand on the ground, and the earth as witness.

A night awake, with a newborn, in a hospital, at a vigil, on a night shift, isn't one thing. There's the early part, when you're still yourself. The deep middle, when the world goes strange and quiet. And the last hours, gray and thin, when something shifts before the light comes. The sutta that tells this night divides it into three watches, like guard shifts. Mara is gone. The wanderer is alone with the dark, and his mind, he says, is calm, clear and steady. Now the real work of the night begins.
screen: `A NIGHT ISN'T ONE THING.` → `THREE WATCHES, LIKE GUARD SHIFTS.` → `THE REAL WORK BEGINS.`

segments.voice: The Buddha describes this night himself, in the same sutta where he told of the austerities. In the first watch, his settled mind turned to memory, and he recalled his past lives: one birth, two, a hundred, a hundred thousand, across the ages. Here I had this name, this family, this food, these joys and pains. There I died, and was born again. Like a traveler remembering every village on a long road. In the second watch, he turned outward. He saw beings everywhere dying and being reborn, and he saw why: they fare according to their actions, kind ones leading one way, cruel ones another. Kamma, the law of action and result, laid open like a landscape seen from a hilltop. In the third watch, the last before dawn, he turned to the root of it all. He saw suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to its ending, directly. And he saw the taints, the deep stains of sensual desire, becoming and ignorance, come to an end. Ignorance was gone, he says; knowledge arose. Darkness was gone; light arose. Notice the order: his own story, then everyone's story, then the thing underneath every story. Buddhists read this in different ways. Traditional teaching takes the past lives as the Buddha's direct memory; some modern readers focus more on the pattern the night reveals. Either way, the text keeps the shape: the night had watches, and each one went deeper.
screen: `FIRST WATCH — HIS OWN PAST LIVES.` · `SECOND — ALL BEINGS AND THEIR DEEDS.` · `THIRD — THE TAINTS COME TO AN END.` · `DARKNESS GONE, LIGHT AROSE.` · then, large: `NIGHT HAS WATCHES.`

segments.voice: Take three slow breaths, one for each watch: on the first, look inward at your own body and mood; on the second, look outward at the people around you, each with their own story, their own actions and results; on the third, look underneath, at the simple fact of breathing beneath every story. Then keep sitting, watching the breath arrive and leave.
Asava. The deep taints, of desire, becoming and ignorance, that ended in the last of the three watches under the tree.
Your line: night has watches. A hard stretch has parts too. Day fifty-four, done.

55.title: Dawn, awake
55.hook: the morning star rises; he is the Buddha, the one who woke up
55.howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, the full moon of the month of Vesakha, and in Japan it is kept as Bodhi Day (Rohatsu) in December, in some Zen communities with meditation through the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asava: the taints, ended in the last of the three watches. Night has watches.

Before a sunrise, there's a stretch when the sky goes from dark to not-dark, and nobody watching can say exactly when it happened. On a camping trip, after a sleepless night, from the window of an early flight, it looks the same. Some mornings, low in the east, one bright point of light hangs on after the other stars have faded: the morning star, the planet Venus. The wanderer has sat through the whole night. The third watch is ending. And the tellings, especially in East Asia, say that as the morning star rose, it was done. Today's word is what he had become.
screen: `BEFORE THE SUN.` → `DARK, THEN NOT-DARK.` → `THE MORNING STAR RISES.`

segments.voice: Buddha isn't a name. It's a description, from the same root as bodhi: budh, to wake up. Buddha means the one who has woken up, the awakened one. The man under the tree was Siddhattha Gotama, a Sakyan, a former prince, a wanderer. At dawn, Buddhists say, he became the Buddha. The suttas tell a story about this very word. Some time later, a brahmin named Dona sees the Buddha's footprints on a road, marked with wheels, and follows them, amazed. He finds him sitting under a tree and asks: are you a god? No, says the Buddha. A heavenly musician? No. A spirit? No. A human being? No. Then what are you? Everything that would make him any of those, the Buddha explains, has been cut off at the root, like a palm tree stump that can't grow again. Like a lotus that grows in the water and rises above it, unsoiled. So remember me, he says, as awake. Traditions remember the day differently. Theravada Buddhists celebrate the awakening on Vesak, a full-moon day that also remembers his birth and his death. In Japan, the day of awakening is kept in December, and some Zen monasteries sit through the night before it, waiting for the morning star. Different calendars, the same dawn, and the same one word. Not a god. Not a spirit. Awake.

Watch the sky change slowly, from black to deep blue to gray to gold, without hurrying it. As the light comes, notice your own awareness, the simple fact that you are awake, right now, seeing.

Your line: awake. One word, and it was what he had become. See you tomorrow.

56.title: The house-builder
56.hook: craving named and seen; the rafters broken, the ridgepole shattered (Dhammapada 153–154)
56.howItsDone: Dhammapada 153–154 are memorized and chanted in Theravada communities, whose tradition holds they were the Buddha's first words after awakening, and teachers use the house-builder to explain craving as the source of rebirth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha: the one who woke up, at dawn, as the morning star rose. Awake.

The same argument, for the tenth time. The same late-night snack. The same reason for not calling someone back. Then one day, instead of just doing it again, you catch it in the act. Oh. There it is. That's the thing that keeps building this. Tradition says that when the Buddha woke, the first words he spoke were a short poem. Not a sermon. Not a rule. A poem to someone he'd been looking for, for a very long time, and finally, he'd found him.
screen: `CATCHING YOURSELF IN A PATTERN.` → `OH. THERE IT IS.` → `A POEM TO SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: The poem is in the Dhammapada, verses one fifty-three and one fifty-four, and it pictures life after life as a house built again and again. Through many births, the Buddha says, he ran on, looking for the builder of this house, and birth again and again was painful. Then, in Max Müller's translation from 1881, he speaks directly to the builder: "maker of the tabernacle, thou hast been seen; thou shalt not make up this tabernacle again." Tabernacle is Müller's old word for the house: a dwelling, a tent. And then: "All thy rafters are broken, thy ridge-pole is sundered." So who is the house-builder? The Buddhist commentaries answer: craving. Tanha, the thirst from day nine, the wanting that keeps building a self and a life around it, over and over. The rafters, they say, are the other stains of the mind. The ridgepole, the beam at the very top that holds up the whole roof, is ignorance. And look at the first verb. Before anything is broken, the builder is seen; the rafters fall after. That's this whole week in one poem: a seat of grass, a vow to stay, Mara's army, the earth as witness, three watches, and dawn. And at the end, one quiet sentence to the one who'd been building the whole time. House-builder, you are seen.

segments.voice: Think of one habit you've already started to see through, something you used to do without noticing: hitting snooze, interrupting, checking the fridge when bored. Picture it as a small builder busy with hammer and nails, and silently speak to it the way the poem does, not angrily, just clearly: I see you. Notice whether seeing it changes anything, then rest with the breath.
The house-builder. Craving, which builds life after life, seen at last by the Buddha: its rafters broken, its ridgepole shattered.
